text: Drawing free body diagrams. The first step in describing and analyzing most phenomena in physics involves the careful drawing of a free body diagram, or FBD. FBDs have been used throughout this chapter. An FBD must only include the external forces acting on the body of interest. Once we have drawn an accurate FBD, we can apply Newton's first law if the body is in equilibrium, Fnet equals zero, or Newton's second law if the body is accelerating. Fnet is not equal to zero. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. Should the net force be drawn as a separate arrow on a free body diagram? Explain why or why not. An MIT OpenCourseWare video is linked on the course web page. This worked example shows how to draw separate free body diagrams for interacting blocks and apply Newton's second law to each system. Constructing free body diagrams. Observe the following rules when constructing an FBD. Draw the object under consideration as a simpler shape, for example point, box, etc. It does not have to be artistic. We often place the object at the origin of an xy coordinate system. Include all forces that act on the object representing these forces as vectors. Do not include the net force on the object. We never include both forces of an action reaction pair. Convert the FBD into a more detailed diagram showing the x and y components of a given force. In this case, place a squiggly line through the original vector to show that it is no longer in play, i.e. replaced by components. If there are more than a single object in the problem, draw a separate FBD for each object. If there is acceleration, we do not directly include it in the FBD. However, it may help to indicate acceleration outside the FBD. Non-academy video is linked on the course webpage. This video shows how to identify all forces acting on an object, represent them with a free body diagram, and resolve angled forces into horizontal and vertical components to determine the net force and resulting motion. Let's apply the problem solving strategy in drawing an FBD for a sled. In the figure, part A, a sled is pulled by force vector P at a 30-degree angle. In part B, we show a free body diagram as described by steps 1 and 2. In part C, we show all forces in terms of their x and y components in keeping with step 3. Example problem. Two blocks on an inclined plane. The problem. Construct the free body diagram for object A and object B in the figure. The worked solution. The model. Objects A and B are treated as separate particles on an inclined plane. The x-axis is chosen parallel to the incline, and the y-axis is chosen perpendicular to the incline. Object A is attached to a cord and is in contact with object B. B is in contact with both object A and the incline. Normal forces act perpendicular to contact surfaces. Friction forces act parallel to contact surfaces, and tension acts along the cord. Each free body diagram includes only forces acting on the isolated object. The math. For object A, the forces acting on the isolated object are its weight vector, W sub A, the tension vector T from the cord, the normal force vector, N sub B A exerted by B on A, and the friction force vector, F sub B A exerted by B on A. For object B, the forces acting on the isolated object are its weight vector, W sub B, the normal force vector, N sub B from the incline, the friction force vector, F sub B from the incline, the normal force vector, N sub AB exerted by A on B, and the friction force vector, F sub AB exerted by A on B. The contact forces between A and B occur in third-law pairs. The corresponding force equation is vector N sub AB equals minus vector N sub B A. Vector F sub AB equals minus vector F sub B A. These pairs act on different objects, so they appear on different free body diagrams. The conclusion. The free body diagram for object A contains vector W sub A, vector T, vector N sub B A, and vector F sub B A. The free body diagram for object B contains vector W sub B, vector N sub B, vector F sub B, vector N sub AB, and vector F sub AB. The problem of object B is essential because action reaction pairs do not cancel within a single object's free body diagram. The problem. A force is applied to two blocks in contact as shown in the figure. Draw the reaction forces between the two blocks. The worked solution follows. The model. The blocks are treated as two separate systems on a horizontal surface. The positive x direction is chosen to the right in the direction of the applied force on block M sub 1. At the contact surface, block M sub 1 pushes on block M sub 2 to the right, while block M sub 2 pushes on block M sub 1 to the left. The prompt asks only for the reaction forces between the blocks, so other forces are not required, unless drawing complete free body diagrams. The math. Newton's third law states that the interaction forces between the two blocks have equal magnitude and opposite direction. If vector A sub 1 2 is the force on block M sub 2 due to block M sub 1, and vector A sub 2 1 is the force on block M sub 1 due to block M sub 2, then vector A sub 1 2 equals minus vector A sub 2 1. Because block M sub 1 pushes block M sub 2 to the right, vector A sub 1 2 points in the positive i-hat direction. The reaction force vector A sub 2 1 therefore points in the negative i-hat direction. The conclusion. The reaction force pair is vector A sub 1 2 on block M sub 2 to the right, and vector A sub 2 1 on block M sub 1 to the left. These forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction, but they act on different blocks, so they do not cancel in either block's individual free body diagram. The problem. A block rests on the table, as shown in the figure. A light rope is attached to it and runs over a pulley. The other end of the rope is attached to a second block. The two blocks are said to be coupled. Block M sub 2 exerts a force due to its weight, which causes the system, two blocks and a string to accelerate. We assume that the string has no mass, so that we do not have to consider it as a separate object. Draw a free body diagram for each block. The model. The two blocks are treated as separate systems connected by a taught, massless rope divided by a frictionless pulley. For block M sub 1, the positive x direction is to the right, toward the pulley, and the positive y direction is upward. For block M sub 2, the positive y direction is upward. The table is treated as frictionless, so no friction force acts on M sub 1. The rope tension has the same magnitude in both diagrams, because the rope is massless, and the pulley is frictionless. Y Newton's second law separately to each block, using plus x to the right for M sub 1 and plus y upward for M sub 2. For block M sub 1, we have for the horizontal motion, some f sub x equals M sub 1 a. T equals M sub 1 a. For block M sub 2 in the vertical direction, some f sub y equals 0, because there is no vertical acceleration. Therefore, N minus M sub 1 g equals 0, so N equals M sub 1 g. For block M sub 2, we have for the vertical motion, some f sub y equals M sub 2 a sub y. T minus M sub 2 g equals negative M sub 2 a. M sub 2 g minus t equals M sub 2 a. Then we can solve the two acceleration tension equations for a in terms of T. T equals M sub 1 a. M sub 2 g minus t equals M sub 2 a. Then we can solve for a and t separately in terms of the masses and g. M sub 2 g minus M sub 1 a equals M sub 2 a. A equals M sub 2 g divided by M sub 1 plus M sub 2. T equals M sub 1 times M sub 2 g divided by M sub 1 plus M sub 2 times g. The conclusion, the free body diagram for M sub 1 contains vector N upward, vector W sub 1 downward, and vector t to the right. The free body diagram for M sub 2 contains vector t upward and vector W sub 2 downward. The two blocks require separate free body diagrams because the forces acting on each block are different, even though their accelerations are linked by the rope. Because the rope is massless and taught over a frictionless pulley, the tension magnitude is the same on both blocks, and the acceleration magnitudes are equal. A equals M sub 2 g divided by M sub 1 plus M sub 2. An organic chemistry tutor video is linked on the course web page. This video gives another worked example of a pulley system, emphasizing separate free body diagrams, shared tension, and the acceleration constraint.
